title: Teach Us to Pray: Prayer, Beelzebul, Jonah, and Woes

verses.text: One day in a place where Jesus had just finished praying, one of His disciples requested, "Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples."
So Jesus told them, "When you pray, say: 'Father, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come.
Give us each day our daily bread.
And forgive us our sins, for we also forgive everyone who sins against us. And lead us not into temptation.'"
Then Jesus said to them, "Suppose one of you goes to his friend at midnight and says, 'Friend, lend me three loaves of bread,
because a friend of mine has come to me on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him.'
And suppose the one inside answers, 'Do not bother me. My door is already shut, and my children and I are in bed. I cannot get up to give you anything.'
I tell you, even though he will not get up to provide for him because of his friendship, yet because of the man's persistence, he will get up and give him as much as he needs.
So I tell you: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you.
For everyone who asks receives; he who seeks finds; and to him who knocks, the door will be opened.
What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will give him a snake instead?
Or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion?
So if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!"
One day Jesus was driving out a demon that was mute. And when the demon was gone, the man who had been mute spoke. The crowds were amazed,
but some of them said, "It is by Beelzebul, the prince of the demons, that He drives out demons."
And others tested Him by demanding a sign from heaven.
Knowing their thoughts, Jesus said to them, "Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and a house divided against a house will fall.
If Satan is divided against himself, how can his kingdom stand? After all, you say that I drive out demons by Beelzebul.
And if I drive out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons drive them out? So then, they will be your judges.
But if I drive out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.
When a strong man, fully armed, guards his house, his possessions are secure.
But when someone stronger attacks and overpowers him, he takes away the armor in which the man trusted, and then he divides up his plunder.
He who is not with Me is against Me, and he who does not gather with Me scatters.
When an unclean spirit comes out of a man, it passes through arid places seeking rest and does not find it. Then it says, 'I will return to the house I left.'
On its return, it finds the house swept clean and put in order.
Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they go in and dwell there. And the final plight of that man is worse than the first."
As Jesus was saying these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said, "Blessed is the womb that bore You, and blessed are the breasts that nursed You!"
But He replied, "Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it."
As the crowds were increasing, Jesus said, "This is a wicked generation. It demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of Jonah.
For as Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites, so the Son of Man will be a sign to this generation.

The Queen of the South will rise at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them; for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and now One greater than Solomon is here.
The men of Nineveh will stand at the judgment with this generation and condemn it; for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and now One greater than Jonah is here.
No one lights a lamp and puts it in a cellar or under a basket. Instead, he sets it on a stand, so those who enter can see the light.
Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eyes are good, your whole body also is full of light. But when they are bad, your body is full of darkness.
Be careful, then, that the light within you is not darkness.
So if your whole body is full of light, with no part of it in darkness, you will be radiant, as though a lamp were shining on you."
As Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee invited Him to dine with him; so He went in and reclined at the table.
But the Pharisee was surprised to see that Jesus did not first wash before the meal.
Then the Lord said, "Now you Pharisees clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness.
You fools! Did not the One who made the outside make the inside as well?
But give as alms the things that are within you, and behold, everything will be clean for you.
Woe to you Pharisees! For you pay tithes of mint, rue, and every herb, but you disregard justice and the love of God. You should have practiced the latter without neglecting the former.
Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the chief seats in the synagogues and the greetings in the marketplaces.
Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, which men walk over without even noticing."
One of the experts in the law told Him, "Teacher, when You say these things, You insult us as well."
"Woe to you as well, experts in the law!" He replied. "For you weigh men down with heavy burdens, but you yourselves will not lift a finger to lighten their load.
Woe to you! For you build tombs for the prophets, but it was your fathers who killed them.
So you are witnesses consenting to the deeds of your fathers: They killed the prophets, and you build their tombs.
Because of this, the wisdom of God said, 'I will send them prophets and apostles; some of them they will kill and others they will persecute.'
As a result, this generation will be charged with the blood of all the prophets that has been shed since the foundation of the world,
from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who was killed between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, all of it will be charged to this generation.
Woe to you experts in the law! For you have taken away the key to knowledge. You yourselves have not entered, and you have hindered those who were entering."
As Jesus went on from there, the scribes and Pharisees began to oppose Him bitterly and to ply Him with questions about many things,
waiting to catch Him in something He might say.

context.author: Traditionally Luke, a Gentile physician and traveling companion of the apostle Paul, who also wrote the book of Acts
context.genre: Teaching and controversy — a short model prayer and encouragement to pray, then a series of confrontations that move from the charge of working by Beelzebul to six woes spoken at a Pharisee's dinner
context.audience: Theophilus and a broad, largely Gentile Greek-speaking readership
context.setting: Luke does not name the place where Jesus was praying or where the later scenes unfold. The setting is the long journey toward Jerusalem that began in chapter 9, and the final scene is a meal in a Pharisee's house.
context.custom: Village houses were small, with one room for the whole family to sleep, so the neighbor who says he and his children are in bed cannot rise without waking everyone. Bread was baked daily, so a family with a surprise guest at night might have nothing left. Pharisaic tradition required washing before a meal beyond what the Law itself commanded for ordinary people, which is why the host is surprised. Tombs were whitewashed or marked so that people would not accidentally touch one and become unclean, and an unmarked grave made people unclean without their knowing it (Numbers 19:16).
context.timelineImmediate: Luke has just shown Mary choosing to listen, and now shows Jesus Himself at prayer, a recurring picture in this Gospel, before the disciple asks to be taught. The Lord's Prayer here is shorter than Matthew's, and the BSB footnotes that later manuscripts expand it to match Matthew's longer form. The chapter then builds in intensity, from a request about prayer to open hostility, ending with the scribes and Pharisees plotting to trap Him.
context.timelineBible: "Hallowed be Your name" recalls Ezekiel 36:23, and "the finger of God" echoes the magicians' admission in Exodus 8:19. The sign of Jonah draws on the book of Jonah, and the Queen of the South is the queen of Sheba, who came to hear Solomon's wisdom (1 Kings 10). "From the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah" spans the Hebrew Bible from Genesis 4 to 2 Chronicles 24, which closes the Hebrew Scriptures.
context.sparkNotes: When a disciple asks Jesus to teach them to pray, He gives a short prayer for God's name, God's kingdom, daily bread, forgiveness, and protection from temptation, then tells of a friend who gets bread at midnight through persistence and promises that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask. After He frees a mute man, critics say He works by Beelzebul, and Jesus answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand, that He casts out demons by the finger of God, and that no one can stay neutral. He refuses any sign but the sign of Jonah and says One greater than Jonah and Solomon is here. At a Pharisee's dinner He pronounces woes on the Pharisees and experts in the law for outward religion that neglects justice and the love of God, and the opposition turns bitter.

translation.meaning: A rare word whose exact meaning is uncertain. It has been understood as "daily," "for the coming day," or "necessary for existence." It appears nowhere else in the New Testament except in Matthew's version of this prayer, and no earlier use of it has been found outside Christian writing.

Literally shamelessness, boldness that does not worry about embarrassment. The friend in the story gets what he asks for because he will not be put off, and Jesus presents that bold persistence as the right way to ask God.

occurrences.note: The only time this word appears in the New Testament.

translation.meaning: A name for the ruler of demons, linked to an old Philistine deity. The BSB notes the Vulgate reads "Beelzebub." Jesus does not argue about the name but about the logic: a kingdom at war with itself cannot last.

otBackground.note: The magicians' words "This is the finger of God" — the phrase Jesus uses in verse 20.

commentary.note: Henry calls "Lord, teach us to pray" "itself a good prayer, and a very needful one, for it is a hard thing to pray well, and it is Jesus Christ only that can teach us, by his word and Spirit, how to pray." On "ask, and it shall be given," he adds that you will receive "either the thing itself or that which is equivalent; either the thorn in the flesh removed, or grace sufficient given in."

Ryle takes the parable of the friend at midnight as a lesson in "the importance of perseverance in prayer," since if boldness succeeds so well between people, "how much more may we expect it to obtain mercies when used in prayer to God." He notes that the Greek word for importunity is used only here in the New Testament, and warns against hunting for "far-fetched allegorical meanings" in the story.

Spurgeon says the disciple's request shows how far Jesus' own prayer lay above anything he had known, and that "if we are to pray aright, we must be taught of God, by his Holy Spirit." We are full of infirmities, and prayer is where we feel them most, but "the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities," so we may breathe this very prayer: "Lord, teach us to pray."

Lewis does not comment on Luke, but in Letters to Malcolm he writes about this prayer. He says that for many years after his conversion he used no ready-made prayers except the Lord's Prayer, and then realized that trying to make it his daily bread meant counting on more mental and spiritual strength than he had. In Letter 5 he offers his own private expansions of it, such as hearing "Thy will be done" as "by me, now," which brings him back to brass tacks. (Paraphrased from secondary summaries; Lewis's works remain under copyright.)

overview.summary: A disciple asks Jesus to teach them to pray, and He gives a short prayer and a lesson on persistence. Accused of casting out demons by Beelzebul, He answers and points to the sign of Jonah. At a Pharisee's meal, He pronounces woes on the religious leaders.
overview.settingLine: The road to Jerusalem, ending at a Pharisee's meal.

history.t: Other Jewish exorcists worked in this era, hence "by whom do your sons cast them out?"
Pharisees were respected for strict purity and tithing, which makes Jesus' woes startling.

customs.t: A village home had one room, so waking for a late guest meant waking the whole family.
Pharisees washed before meals for purity, so Jesus skipping it was noticed.

archaeology.t: Excavations uncovered Assyria's great palaces and a library of clay tablets.
Stepped baths found across Judea reflect the purity concern behind these meals.

overview.discussion: Jesus said to ask, seek and knock, yet some prayers go unanswered. How do we read that promise honestly?
overview.book: The third Gospel · 24 chapters. Written as an orderly account, with Acts as its sequel.
